hints: Look at chromatogram A and find the two distances you need - from the line of origin to the centre of the beta-carotene spot, and from the line of origin to the solvent front.

Recall the formula $R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by pigment}}{\text{distance moved by solvent}}$ and check that your answer has no units and is just below 1.0 because beta-carotene is very close to the front.
walkthrough:
Recall What Rf Means**
Rf tells you how far a pigment travelled relative to the solvent. Both distances are measured from the line of origin. So $R_f = \frac{\text{distance pigment moved}}{\text{distance solvent moved}}$. It always has no units and is always less than 1.

Apply To Beta-Carotene**
In Fig. 3.1 A, beta-carotene has moved almost as far as the solvent front, so the top distance is almost equal to the bottom distance. Dividing gives about 0.95. That high value fits because beta-carotene is very non-polar and very soluble in the ether-cyclohexane solvent, so it travels with the front.

hints: Compare A and B side by side - which spots have disappeared or changed name, and what is different about how far the solvent front has moved up the plate?
Link the method description to the labels - what does replacing magnesium with two hydrogen ions do to chlorophyll, and what would stopping the run early do to all distances?
walkthrough:
Spot The Solvent Front Difference**
In B the solvent front is much lower down the plate than in A, even though the plate size looks the same. That means B was not left to run as long. It was stopped early, so all spots have had less time to separate and move.

Explain The New Pigments**
Method B treated the extract with a chemical that swaps the single magnesium ion in the chlorophyll porphyrin head for two hydrogen ions. That product is called phaeophytin. So chlorophyll a disappears and phaeophytin a appears instead. Chlorophyll b is also partly changed to phaeophytin b, while beta-carotene, remaining chlorophyll b and xanthophyll stay similar.

Final answer: 1. Chromatogram B was run for less time / stopped early, so solvent front has moved a shorter distance. 2. Chlorophyll a has been converted to phaeophytin a (and chlorophyll b partly to phaeophytin b) by replacement of Mg2+ with 2H+.

hints: Remember Rf is not a fixed constant like relative molecular mass - it depends on the exact conditions of the separation, so think what was different in the other lab's setup.
walkthrough:
Why Rf Varies Between Labs**
Rf depends on how strongly the pigment sticks to the stationary phase versus how well it dissolves in the mobile phase. If you change the solvent mixture, change the type of TLC plate, or run at a different temperature, solubility and attraction change, so the same pigment travels a different relative distance.
Final answer: A different solvent system or different stationary phase / TLC plate material or different temperature was used.

hints: Start by tracing the solid line for chlorophyll a and the dotted line for carotenoids across Fig. 3.2 - where on the wavelength axis do both lines rise together and where do both stay near zero?
Now look for where they separate - compare heights between 400-445 nm and 445-525 nm, and check the red end around 640-680 nm.
Pick out exact peak values to make your comparison precise - note the highest blue peak for each and count how many peaks each curve has.
Structure your answer as paired similarities and differences with wavelength ranges and percentage absorption, not just colour names.
walkthrough:
Find The Similarities**
Both curves are high on the left in the blue region, roughly 400 to 475 nm. Both then fall to near zero between about 525 and 600 nm in the green-yellow region. That means neither pigment usefully absorbs green-yellow light.

Compare The Blue Region Carefully**
They do not overlap exactly. Chlorophyll a (solid line) is higher from about 400 to 445 nm, peaking near 425-430 nm. Carotenoids (dotted line) take over from about 445 to 525 nm, with higher absorption and peaks near 460-465 nm and near 495 nm.

Spot The Big Red Difference**
On the right side, chlorophyll a shows a clear red peak between about 640 and 680 nm, peaking near 665 nm. Carotenoids stay at almost zero there. So chlorophyll a has a blue peak plus a red peak (two main peaks), while carotenoids have only blue-region peaks (three small peaks) and no red peak. This is why carotenoids act as accessory pigments broadening the range for photosynthesis.

Final answer: Similarities: both absorb blue light 400-475 nm; both absorb little / no green-yellow light 525-600 nm. Differences: chlorophyll a absorbs at more wavelengths overall; chlorophyll a absorbs more between 400-445 nm with peak about 66% at 425 nm; carotenoids absorb more between 445-525 nm with peaks about 60% at 460 nm and 56% at 495 nm; chlorophyll a absorbs red light 640-680 nm with peak about 47% at 665 nm, carotenoids do not; chlorophyll a has two main peaks (blue and red), carotenoids have three blue peaks and no red peak.

hints: Start where gibberellin is made - in the embryo - and think where it needs to travel to switch on digestive enzymes.
Recall the receptor mechanism inside aleurone cells involving DELLA protein and a transcription factor - what is released when DELLA is broken down?
Link that released factor to gene expression - which hydrolytic enzymes are made and what substrate do they attack?
Finish the causal chain by explaining why the embryo needs the products - what process needs glucose and maltose?
walkthrough:
From Embryo To Aleurone**
Light stimulates the embryo to make gibberellin. Gibberellin diffuses to the aleurone layer, the living protein-rich layer around the starchy endosperm. Think of it as the messenger telling the food store to release nutrients.

Switching On The Gene**
In aleurone cells gibberellin binds to its receptor GID1. This triggers breakdown of DELLA protein, which was blocking gene expression. Once DELLA is gone, a transcription factor called PIF is freed and switches on genes for hydrolytic enzymes such as alpha-amylase and protease.

Mobilising The Store For Growth**
Amylase is secreted into the endosperm and hydrolyses starch to maltose, then to glucose. Those soluble sugars diffuse to the embryo and are used in respiration to release ATP for cell division and elongation, so the radicle can emerge and the seedling can grow.

Final answer: Gibberellin moves to / acts on aleurone layer; binds to gibberellin receptor / GID1; causes breakdown of DELLA protein; releasing PIF / transcription factor; which switches on genes for amylase / maltase / protease; amylase hydrolyses starch to maltose; sugars / glucose used for respiration / growth of embryo.
